messages.body_plain:
That's very helpful Marc. I was just experiencing this exact same issue (terribly slow mixing) on a similar model so I hope this offers some relief...

Out of curiosity, could we easily extend this Poisson random effects model to multiple surveys by simply adding another index loop for visits?

Taking your example, now with J = 3 visits, and a desire to estimate an overall rate of change across years, could I not do something like...

# Likelihood

# State process

for (t in 1:T) {

  for(i in 1:M){

    for(j in 1:J){

      C[i,j,t] ~ dpois(lambda[i,j,t])

      log(lambda[i,j,t]) <- site.eff[i] + r*year[t]

    }

  }

}

Also, I haven't explored it in-depth, but I think the `gamlss` package (coupled with the `gamlss.dist` package) allows the fitting of some random effects double Poisson models of Barker et al (2018); at least I get similar parameter estimates for their model using gamlss...

Again, using your example, after making appropriate changes to the data structure:

gamlss(C ~ 1 + random(site), family = DPO)

I don't suppose there's any JAGS/BUGS code out there for the double Poisson?

Thanks,
Adam Smith

On Monday, June 4, 2018 at 10:16:13 AM UTC-4, marc.kery wrote:
> Dear all,
>
> I want to share a little personal discovery I just made. Lately, I have been experimenting with variants of Poisson random-effects models, which have been found to be just fantastic for count data (e.g., Barker et al., 2018, Link et al. 2018). I simulated non-robust-design data for M sites and T years and then fit a model with random site plus random year effects. This was almost impossible to get to convergence with JAGS in my original formulation, which was this (shown for the site effects only) :
>
> # Specify model in BUGS language
>
> cat(file = "model1.txt","
>
> model {
>
> # Priors
> mu.lambda ~ dunif(-6, 6)
>
> for(i in 1:M){
>
>   site.eff[i] ~ dnorm(0, tau.site)
>
> }
>
> tau.site <- pow(sd.site, -2)
>
> sd.site ~ dunif(0, 10)
>
>
>
> # Likelihood
> for(i in 1:M){
>
>   for(t in 1:T){
>
>     C[i,t] ~ dpois(lambda[i,t])
>
>     log(lambda[i,t]) <- mu.lambda + site.eff[i]
>   }
>
> }
>
>
> Mixing for the chains for the intercept was just abismal ! In contrast, when I put the mean back into the Normal distribution for the site random effects, mixing became just great. That's this parameterization of the same model:
>
> # Specify model in BUGS language
>
> cat(file = "model2.txt","
>
> model {
>
> # Priors
> for(i in 1:M){
>
>   site.eff[i] ~ dnorm(mu.lambda, tau.site)
>
> }
>
> mu.lambda ~ dunif(-6, 6)
>
> tau.site <- pow(sd.site, -2)
>
> sd.site ~ dunif(0, 10)
>
>
>
> # Likelihood
>
> # State process
>
> for(i in 1:M){
>
>   for(t in 1:T){
>
>     C[i,t] ~ dpois(lambda[i,t])
>     log(lambda[i,t]) <- site.eff[i]
>
>   }
>
> }
>
>
> I think the latter is called 'hierarchical centering' and has been known to lead to better mixing in MCMC (see Gelman books). Good to remember before you bang your head against the wall !
>
> Best regards  ---- Marc
>

messages.body_plain:
Dear Adam,

yes, you can do exactly that: constraining the annual effects to be a log-linear function of the year to estimate an overall trend.

Of course, with 3 reps and assuming, among other things, population closure and not too wild unexplained heterogeneity, you could use a static N-mixture model (with years as strata) or a dynamic N-mixture model (a.k.a. Dail-Madsen model) to make inference about true abundance. Because in spite of what some recent publications claim, the binomial N-mixture model has a pretty good track record for doing that.

Not sure about the double Poisson, but I'd be surprised if this couldn't be done in BUGS.

Best regards  ---- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marc,

See Monnahan, C.C., Thorson, J.T., & Branch, T.A. (2016) Faster estimation of Bayesian models in ecology using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 8, 339-348. Your first block  of code is similar to their non-centered version (though they do N(0,1) and multiple by SD), the second centered. They found centered to be generally faster in JAGS and non-centered faster (and fewer divergences) in Stan.

Regards, Mike

messages.subject: Graduate Research Associate in Quantitative Ecology at Patuxent Wildlife Research Center: Capture-recapture analysis of black-duck banding and recapture data
messages.subject_clean: Graduate Research Associate in Quantitative Ecology at Patuxent Wildlife Research Center: Capture-recapture analysis of black-duck banding and recapture data
messages.body_plain:
hi all,
 We're looking to hire a part-time (abt 20 hrs per week) graduate student assistant to work up to 12 months on a project which involves developing CJS-type models ("Brownie models") for waterfowl band recover data.  This is a really unique data set (see attached description) and a great opportunity for a motivated and ambitious student in quantitative ecology. There are a couple of clear papers to be written as part of this project that will have impact. The data set is clean and tidy.

 The position would involve a stay here at PWRC for a few weeks but could otherwise be done at your home institution during the academic year.

 You need to be extremely proficient with R, have experience with BUGS, and have experience or at least knowledge of CJS/Brownie models. Interest in waterfowl population biology and management is a plus.

more details attached.

 Do not respond to this email address!

regards
andy

messages.subject: AHM examples converted to NIMBLE
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

We have converted most of the BUGS/JAGS examples from Kéry and Royle's Applied Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology Volume I to run in NIMBLE.

The examples are available here: https://github.com/nimble-dev/AHMnimble.  Scroll down on that page for more explanation.

Note that to see the html results comparing NIMBLE and JAGS, you will need to download the repository from GitHub and open the html pages.  GitHub itself will show you the html source, not the rendered pages.

NIMBLE uses (almost) the same modeling language as WinBUGS/OpenBUGS/JAGS, so in most cases converting examples is pretty easy. There are a few cases remaining to be fixed.  Many of the examples could be improved with NIMBLE customizations.

Please contribute to this effort!

Apologies for the general advertisement.  We hope this is relevant to many members of this list.

-Perry

messages.subject_clean: CJS model with m-array formulation with missing visits
messages.body_plain:
Hi guys,

Is it possible to fit the Cormack-Jolly-Seber model with the m-array formulation (described e.g. in the BPA book from Marc & Michael) in case of missing visits/occasions (i.e. with NAs in the observations)? It is easily possible with capture histories, but it seems that with m-arrays NA would be taken as zero which is not good. Did you find solution for this or did you just use individual capture histories?

Tomas

PS: perhaps the workaround could be to make a specific m-array row for each pattern of NAs in the data.. Or, specific m-array for each site. Would you use this solution or is there something simpler?

messages.subject: Re: CJS model with m-array formulation with missing visits
messages.subject_clean: CJS model with m-array formulation with missing visits
messages.body_plain:
Dear Tomas,

if there are missing values for some occasions for all individuals simultaneously, then it appears to me that this is quite easy: you simply set to zero the recapture probability for those occasions.

If on the other hand the missing-value pattern is individual-specific, then it would become a little more involved for the m-array formulation of the model. But I find it hard to envision a sampling situation that would produce such data.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.subject_clean: Framework for simulation study to validate bayesian models
messages.body_plain:
Hi guys,

I am looking for a framework that would allow to take JAGS/bugs model
and on many sets of simulated data test if there is a bias (or not) in
the parameter estimates (the real parameters would be known because
the data are simulated). Is there any such framework? I've seen only
`run.jags.study()` in R package `runjags`, but this is focused on
crossvalidation. I need to check the bias in parameter estimates.

Or, can you remind me a chapter in one of Marc's book which focuses on
that? :-) I am especially interested how to evaluate the bias across
the generated data sets.

Thanks in advance!

Tomas

messages.subject: Re: Framework for simulation study to validate bayesian models
messages.subject_clean: Framework for simulation study to validate bayesian models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tomas,

It sounds like you want to run a standard model-validation exercise. The process is similar regardless of the type of model you want to fit, and I'm sure there are R packages available to help with this, although I haven't used any. I would perform the following steps:

1. Simulate the data (1000 times or so, or probably a minimum of 100 if your model takes very long to run). You can simulate the data in base R or your package/program of choice - no need to simulate in a BUGS framework. Chapter 4 of Kery & Royle (vol 1) could help with this.

2. To each simulated dataset, fit your BUGS model, making sure to output the estimates of the parameters that you want to validate.

3. Across all the simulated datasets, check how many times the 95% BCI of each estimate contains your true value. If the 95% BCI excludes the true value >5% of the time, you have a bias (probably a big one if your 95% BCI is fairly wide). You can check whether the true value is above or below each BCI to evaluate the direction of the bias.

4. As an additional way to evaluate the estimates, across all the simulated datasets, take the mean of the parameter estimate and calculate a 95% CI based on the SD across datasets. If the 95% CI excludes your true value, you have a bias. (This is mixing Bayesian and frequentist paradigms, which is not ideal, and I hope someone will correct me if this comparison will be fundamentally flawed - I've only implemented it in a purely frequentist framework. My thought is that it might detect smaller biases than could be detected from the 95% BCI, if there is high uncertainty in the model, as is common in a Bayesian framework. But perhaps precision around the mean could be overestimated with this method, especially with many replicates, so it would be worth considering the biological significance of any bias.)

I would personally run step 2 in JAGS with runjags as usual for any model/dataset, and use base R for the other steps. I'll look forward to hearing suggestions from anyone who knows an efficient R package or has any BUGS-specific advice.

Cheers,

Emily

Emily Weiser
La Crosse, WI
Emily.L...@gmail.com
https://sites.google.com/site/emilylweiser/
http://birding-by-bike.blogspot.com
